titre: Spinach and Iron: The Decimal Point Legend, and the Legend of Its Debunking
accroche: A misplaced decimal point is said to have inflated spinach's iron. Both the story and the debunking are incomplete: for a 2016 study, it all starts with two analyses (1846, 1848).
contenu_vulgarise:
In the Christmas 1981 issue of the *British Medical Journal*, the cancer specialist Terence Hamblin opens an article on scientific fraud with an anecdote. Popeye swallows spinach for its iron, he writes, but German chemists are said to have shown in the 1930s that the first analysts had put the decimal point in the wrong place, hence a content overestimated by a factor of ten. The sailor would have done better to chew the tin cans. The tale, repeated in many books and magazines, has become the textbook example of an error that spreads.

## A Debunking That Did Not Look Everywhere

Hamblin cites no reference. In 2010, the criminologist Mike Sutton follows the trail and finds neither a misplaced decimal point nor German chemists of the 1930s. He attributes the too-high values to measurement problems and argues that the decimal point story was invented. He also notes that, in the earliest comics, Popeye's spinach is not linked to iron: a 1932 strip credits it with vitamin A. This debunking goes viral.

But Sutton had explored few German and French sources. In 2016, Michael Mielewczik and Janine Moll reopen the literature, including those texts, and reconstruct a different story.

## Two Samples Are Enough

The iron in spinach appears in a table published in 1846 by Louis Saalmüller, who analyzes the plant's ash, then in an analysis by Richardson published in 1848. Each rests on a single sample, and according to Mielewczik and Moll, the whole first wave of iron-rich spinach rests on nothing more. These values are copied from textbook to textbook. In 1852, an anonymous German encyclopedia entry describes spinach for the first time as rich in iron.

In 1892, the physiologist Gustav von Bunge, in Basel, redoes the measurements. He writes, in German, that a figure in Emil von Wolff's table, half a gram of iron per 100 g of dried leaves, is 16 times too high. He still considers spinach useful for iron, but in much smaller amounts.

The gap, from ten to sixteen times depending on the figures, is therefore real and was pointed out as early as the 19th century. Its cause is less certain: a decimal point, a contaminated sample, a confusion between fresh and dry matter.

## The Decimal Point Had a Past

Sutton thought the decimal point story had been fabricated in the 1970s by Arnold Bender, then spread by Hamblin. Mielewczik and Moll show that the idea of a figure overestimated by a factor of ten circulates much earlier. A 1960 German article, cited by them, states that fresh spinach contains 30 to 40 mg of iron per kilo, that is, 3 to 4 mg per 100 g, and not 300 to 400 as many textbooks still say. The story then passes into the German-language press of the 1960s, and then into British and American newspapers in the late 1970s. Hamblin is therefore not its inventor.

## Who Was at Fault?

Mielewczik and Moll conclude that the myth owes less to a faulty scholar than to the quality of the editorial oversight at the journals that published the original data.

What is a debunking worth, then, if it has barely opened the sources of the language in which the error was born?

repere.texte: The whole first wave of iron-rich spinach rested on the results of only two studies, each based on a single sample (Saalmüller, 1846; Richardson, 1848).
repere.source: Mielewczik and Moll, Annals of the History and Philosophy of Biology, vol. 21, 2016, pp. 79-80 (retranslated from the French; original wording not retrieved)

carte.punch: A misplaced decimal point supposedly made spinach a mine of iron. Its debunking is incomplete.
carte.idee: The first wave of iron-rich spinach rests on just two analyses from 1846 and 1848, each on a single sample. The gap, from ten to sixteen times depending on the figures, is real. The decimal point meant to explain it is not demonstrated, and the 2010 debunking of the story's origin was incomplete.

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Hamblin T. J., “Fake.”, British Medical Journal, 1981 (Christmas issue)
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The article that made the decimal point legend worldwide; the text is digitized as page images.

quiz.question: According to Mielewczik and Moll, why did the too-high iron value for spinach survive in textbooks?
choix: Because no one had measured the iron in spinach before the 1960s
Because Bunge never published his 1892 correction
Because two isolated analyses were copied from textbook to textbook
Because the 19th-century measurements were redone and confirmed
quiz.explication: The values of 1846 and 1848, drawn from two samples, were copied for decades, and the authors blame the editorial oversight at the original journals more than a faulty scholar. The iron in spinach had been measured well before 1960, Bunge published his correction in 1892, and the redone measurements showed much lower values.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Mike Sutton in 2010, what does the first Popeye comic of 1932 credit spinach with, rather than iron?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Sutton notes that, in the earliest comics, Popeye's spinach is not linked to iron: a 1932 strip credits it with vitamin A, not iron.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How many samples do the two analyses of 1846 and 1848, at the origin of spinach's reputation as rich in iron, rest on?
choix: Several hundred samples each, collected across Europe
About ten samples each, chosen at random
No real sample: both analyses were theoretical
quiz_supplementaire.explication: According to Mielewczik and Moll, Saalmüller's table (1846) and Richardson's analysis (1848) each rest on a single sample, yet were copied from textbook to textbook.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Gustav von Bunge in 1892, by how many times was the figure in Emil von Wolff's table too high?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Bunge writes that half a gram of iron per 100 g of dried leaves, a figure from von Wolff's table, is 16 times too high, while still judging spinach useful for iron, in smaller amounts.
